title: Marvel Regrew Wolverine From His Skeleton — A Real Flatworm Only Needs One Cell
youtube_description:
Marvel's most ridiculous healing feat is easy next to a real flatworm.

In Wolverine #43 (2006), a Civil War tie-in, Logan hunts down Nitro, the villain behind the Stamford explosion. Nitro detonates at full power and strips every ounce of flesh off Wolverine's bones. A few pages later he's back: muscle, skin, the lot. The usual explanation is that his healing factor lives in his bone marrow, sealed inside an adamantium skeleton nothing can break. Fans still argue it's the most broken power feat Marvel ever drew.

Nature already does something wilder. The planarian is a flatworm about the length of a fingernail. In 1898, biologist Thomas Hunt Morgan cut planarians into pieces and found that a fragment just 1/279th of the worm could grow back into a complete animal: head, brain, gut, everything.

In 2011, researchers in Peter Reddien's lab went further. They took worms whose own stem cells had been wiped out by radiation and transplanted a single stem cell from another worm. That one cell multiplied and replaced the host's tissues, rebuilding the whole body. Wolverine needed his entire skeleton to come back. The flatworm needs one cell.

This channel covers the real science behind Marvel's most ridiculous powers. Subscribe for more of them.

Sources: Marvel Database (Wolverine Vol 3 #43); The Node, "Forgotten classics: T. H. Morgan and planarian regeneration"; Wagner, Wang & Reddien, "Clonogenic Neoblasts Are Pluripotent Adult Stem Cells That Underlie Planarian Regeneration," Science 332 (2011).
